content.title: About
content.content: Chicken thigh is the meat from the upper part of a bird's leg. When stewed with liquid and spices, the meat becomes tender and the skin left on adds extra flavor and richness. This dish is commonly served as a hot main course.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken thighs contain more fat than chicken breast, making them juicier when cooked.
Stewing is one of the oldest cooking methods, preserving nutrients while softening tough meat.
Chicken skin is rich in collagen, which imparts flavor and aroma even though some collagen breaks down with heat.
In many traditional cuisines (e.g., Russian, Polish, American) stewed chicken thighs are often cooked with vegetables and tomato‑based sauces.
When cooked properly, thigh meat stays tender even after long simmering.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Chicken thigh provides complete protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It supplies vitamin B6 and niacin, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Thigh meat contains iron, zinc, and phosphorus important for blood health and bones.

items.title: Beneficial fats
items.content: Although fattier than breast meat, chicken thigh includes a portion of polyunsaturated fatty acids.

items.title: Collagen from skin
items.content: The skin retained in the stew adds collagen, which may help skin and joint health.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Stewed thighs can be calorie‑dense; portion control is advisable for weight‑watching individuals.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: If the recipe uses soy sauce or added salt, sodium can become elevated.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: A small number of people may be allergic to chicken proteins.

items.title: Bacterial contamination risk
items.content: Ensure the meat reaches an internal temperature of at least 74 °C to eliminate salmonella.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the stewed thighs hot, often with a side of potatoes, rice, or vegetables. The skin can be eaten together with the meat or removed for a leaner option. The dish is eaten with a fork and knife.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the stew to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑sized bags for 2‑3 months. Reheat thoroughly before serving.
